doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: Arrangements and recording process
summary: The composers are the arrangers; she records harmonies and talking parts first and sings lead after, and struggles to know when vocals are done.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: The recordings I’ve listened to are — I’ll relate another thing I remember reading. Milt Hinton, the bassist, talking about recording sessions with Dinah Washington and the quartet would get there ahead of time and sort of run through the tunes and then she’d walk in and say, “Okay what have we got?” And she would do one take and consider it done. So this long intro to my question is how do your arrangements occur, which are quite precise at times?

Well the composers are the arrangers and some of what they do is very precise and meant to be played as written. And then there are other spots that are left loose because they know the personality of the people who are going to be on the session in most cases. And they want that person to be able to play a little solo or to do something that has a certain vibe but they don’t dictate exactly what it is.
Are you in a booth singing with the group usually? Or do you sometimes sing after the fact?

Well I mean I have sung along many times with them but I consider it like, it’s not a natural process so to speak. It’s like making a film, you put the pieces together and I generally sing after the fact but of course I do a lot of vocal harmonies that often I will record the vocal, the pads, the vocal harmonies that I’m singing with myself ahead of time and also I do these talking sections as you’ve noticed probably, and I’ll do that ahead of time too because when the band comes in to play it brings them into the atmosphere of the tune kind of. Like the harmonies are such a big part of the feeling of the story that I discovered that it’s nice to do them first. And it’s also nice to do them first for me singing the lead.
Are you a person who has trouble knowing when things are done?
Either your own lyrics or a recording?

My own lyrics not so much. I pretty well know that they’re done although what happens is that I never just sit down and hammer away until something is done. I’ll have an idea and then once I’m in the head of writing the song, the lyrics, it flows through my consciousness all the time and things come up, I’ll find little internal rhymes and rhythms, alliteration and just words that I want to use instead of other words, but once I finish it it’s pretty much done. I’m not rigid about it but singing wise I do have trouble knowing when it’s done. Like I’ll go like I don’t really like the way I sang. Like, “No it’s fine, Lorraine.” But I” — “No, it’s fine.” Once I was doing this album called “Tales of the Unusual” and I wrote lyrics to Nino Rota’s “Juliet of the Spirits” thing called “Rose Aurata.” Russell arranged it for me. It’s mostly in harmony and then there’s this little one talking part where it’s a woman in the circus and she says, “Look at all the people out there tonight, darling, I think we have a full house. I’m so excited.” I was working at the time with Carlos Rosario, the engineer/producer who did a lot of my albums and he’s wonderful. And every time we listened to that back he’d laugh. He says, “It’s just so funny the way you said it.” I said, “Well let me do it again.” And he went, “No, I refuse to let you do it again.” So yeah, I’m not sure a lot of the time if I’m done or not vocally.
